Acting on several rows at once. Tick the box on any row — or press x to tick the focused one and move to the next, X for everything the current filter shows. A bulk bar appears above the list with Set checking, Re-check, Open, Copy links and Delete. Deletes go to the trash like any other, and a row that has changed since the report was built is skipped and reported rather than deleted, so a stale list cannot remove the wrong bookmark. Ticks survive a filter change, so the bar says how many of them the current filter is hiding and offers to drop those. Esc clears the selection without leaving the view.

Working through a list one at a time. Filtering to Broken and getting forty rows tells you what is wrong and then leaves every fix costing the same three moves: find the row again after the list re-renders, aim at its action, decide. Work through in the toolbar, or f, puts one row on screen at a time with its actions large and the rest of the page out of the way — re-check (p), open (Enter), delete (d), skip (j), and k to go back. It starts at the row your cursor is on rather than the top, because the way in is usually "I am looking at this one". Esc leaves, putting the cursor on the row you had reached, so dipping in for three fixes and back out is not a mode switch. It is the same list and the same actions throughout — nothing here is available only in this mode — and stepping past either end says so rather than quietly wrapping round to the start.

Ten links, two minutes. Work through is also offered rather than only waited for: when enough links want attention, a card in the corner of the dashboard names what is waiting — “10 links to review: 4 broken, 3 never opened, 3 not opened in a year” — and Start runs a session over the worst ten. A session ends: it says how many you dealt with, offers another ten while more are waiting, and Done for today puts the offer away until tomorrow. Skipping is not handling, so the count at the end is honest.

Rot report in the toolbar answers the other question this view can be asked. The list says what to fix now; the report says what has been happening to the collection — what has gone without saying so, what has moved or been rewritten, what has been failing for over a month, what is broken and never opened, and what broke this week. Everything in it is already in the report; what was missing was somewhere it added up.
config.helpHealthStatsBody:
Monitored bookmarks keep a history. Their rows add a heartbeat bar of recent checks, uptime over 24 hours, and a response-time sparkline. The uptime percentage is followed by the number of checks behind it, because 100% from three checks and 100% from three hundred are not the same claim. The ⤢ button on the monitor strip — or i on the selected row — opens the full picture: a large response-time chart with minimum, average, and maximum marked, the three uptime windows side by side, and the outage list with when each started, how long it lasted, and what went wrong. A window with no samples reads no data rather than 0%, so a monitor switched on an hour ago is not mistaken for a day of downtime.

All monitors together. The Monitored filter adds a panel above the list answering what the individual rows cannot: how the whole set is doing. It shows pooled uptime over 24 hours, 7 days and 30 days, how many monitors are responding right now, and the average response time across all of them. Uptime here counts checks rather than averaging each monitor's percentage — otherwise a monitor with three recorded checks would weigh as heavily as one with three thousand.

Beneath it are three lists. Least available (7 days) names the monitors with the worst record, with anything failing right now placed first; monitors at a clean 100% are left out, so a short list means little is wrong rather than that only five were examined. Slower than last week compares each monitor's response time over the last day against the seven days before it, listing only meaningful slowdowns — the two windows never overlap, and a handful of checks on either side is not treated as evidence. Outages is every recorded failure across the collection, newest first, each naming the bookmark it belonged to; when there are more than the list shows, it says how many there were in total.

Health over time. Once the health view has been opened on more than one day, a chart beside the text explaining the filter draws the share of healthy bookmarks as a line, with an arrow beside the percentage in the header saying how far it has moved across the recorded window — up 12 points over 30 days. Point at any day to read out its date and the share that was healthy on it; a day with no reading says so rather than showing 0%. The chart is drawn on a fixed 0–100 scale, marked at 100%, so a collection sitting between 91% and 93% looks as flat as it is. One point is recorded per day, kept for 90 days, and days the dashboard was not opened leave a gap in the line rather than a straight segment through them. Nothing is shown until there are at least two days to compare, and the ℹ beside the chart explains the scale and the gaps.

Exports. The toolbar's Export gives the current state of each bookmark in the filtered list; when that list contains monitored bookmarks it also carries their interval, the three uptime windows, last response time and total checks recorded. Uptime is written as a plain number so a spreadsheet can average the column, and a window with no samples is left blank rather than written as zero. Export history, on the Monitored filter, is the other kind of record: one row per individual check with its timestamp, whether the site was up, the ping time, and the HTTP status — for charting an outage or seeing exactly when a site started getting slow.
config.helpHealthExpectBody:
A reachability check asks one question: did the host answer? A shop that answers with "Database connection failed" answers perfectly well, and a plain monitor calls it healthy.

Open the availability popover on a monitored row and an Expected response section sits under the interval. Two narrower tests, both optional:

  • Text the page must contain. Type a phrase that only appears when the page is working — a product name, a heading, the label on a button. Matching ignores capitalisation, so type it as you remember it.
  • Fail if present instead flips it round: healthy while the phrase is missing. Use it for an error banner, a "scheduled maintenance" notice, or a parked-domain message.
  • Status codes that count as healthy. By default anything below 500 counts as reachable, because 401 and 403 are normal for pages behind a login. Name the codes yourself — 200, 200-299, 200,301,401 — when only certain answers are right. A code nextDash cannot read is dropped rather than obeyed, so a typo cannot take a working bookmark down.

Failures like these get their own Content tile and filter, separate from Broken. The distinction is the point: a server that is down and a checkout button that vanished need different responses, and lumping them together hides which one you have. The row says which phrase or code it was expecting, so the reason is on screen rather than in your memory.

Only monitored bookmarks carry these, and only monitored bookmarks read the page body — the checks are the monitor’s. Clearing both fields clears the failure they caused, so a bookmark does not stay red for a rule you removed.
config.helpHealthCertBody:
An expiring certificate is invisible to an ordinary check: the site works perfectly until the morning it does not, and then everything on that domain breaks at once.

Every monitored check over HTTPS already completes a TLS handshake, so nextDash reads the expiry date from it. Nothing to switch on, and no extra request — it is a by-product of the check that was happening anyway.

A Certificates tile appears in the health view once something is close, and the affected rows carry a badge with the days remaining. Warnings go out at 30, 7 and 3 days through the same webhook and push notifications as downtime — three marks rather than a daily countdown, because a reminder every morning for a month is how a warning becomes wallpaper.

Certificates belong to a host, not a bookmark: ten bookmarks on one domain share one, so they all show the badge and one renewal clears the lot. Renewing re-arms the warnings, so the next expiry is announced from scratch.
config.helpHealthDriftBody:
A bookmark can answer 200 OK forever while the page behind it quietly stops being the page you saved. A blog post gets replaced by a category listing, a product page starts redirecting to the shop's front page, a domain lapses and a parking company puts a for-sale notice where your article used to be. None of that trips a reachability check or a keyword rule you have not thought to write — the host is still up, it is just not that page any more. This is what drift watches for.

Turn it on per bookmark: open the availability popover on a monitored row and tick Watch for redirects, retitling and rewrites, underneath the expected-response fields. The very next check becomes the baseline — where the link landed, what the page was titled, and a rough fingerprint of what it said. Every check after that compares the current page against that baseline, never against the previous check, so a page that changes slowly does not drift past the alarm one imperceptible step at a time.

  • Redirect drift. The check already follows redirects, so where it lands costs nothing extra to compare. A different host entirely is the strongest signal; landing on the same site's front page instead of the saved article is the next; a different page on the same host is the weakest, and cosmetic changes — http becoming https, www. appearing or disappearing, a trailing slash, a language prefix, a tracking parameter — are deliberately ignored, or every redirect on the internet would trip this.
  • Title drift. The preview title is already fetched for every check. A title that becomes something like "Domain for sale", "Account suspended" or "404 — Page not found" is called out by name, because that phrase alone is nearly always the whole story. A title that merely changed — a rewrite, a rebrand — is flagged too, but more gently: sites retitle pages for ordinary reasons, so this is a prompt to glance at it, not a verdict. Gaining or losing a site-name suffix ("Intro" next to "Intro | Acme Docs") is not treated as a change at all.
  • Content drift. The strongest and fiddliest signal. The page body is reduced to its most common words and compared against the baseline's — not byte for byte, which would trip on a footer date or a visitor counter, but closely enough that a page which became a different page in substance stands out from one that just changed in small ways.

One check can only report one finding, and redirect beats title beats content — if the link now points at a different host entirely, that is the whole story, and there is no need to also say the title changed. The row's badge names it briefly (Moved, Retitled, Changed); hovering it, or opening the row, shows the full sentence — "Now redirects to shop.example", "Page title now reads Domain for sale". A Drift tile and filter collect everything currently flagged. If the page goes back to matching the baseline, the finding clears itself the same way a recovered outage does; the baseline itself is never quietly replaced by a drifted page, so a bookmark cannot end up drifting one small step at a time without ever raising a flag.

Reading the page body is the one part of a check that costs real bandwidth, which is why this is opt-in and monitored-only: a bookmark that never turns it on pays nothing for the feature, and Periodic checking does not read bodies at all.

Accepting a change you meant to happen. A finding is a prompt, not a verdict: a rebrand, a docs reorganisation, a deliberate move to a new domain all trip drift on every bookmark pointing at that site at once, and all of them are fine. Tick the rows and use Accept drift in the bulk bar — it appears only when the selection actually contains findings, and counts just those. Accepting does two things in one go: it clears the finding, and it drops the baseline the finding was measured against, so the next check records the page as it is today. Clearing only the finding would not work — the stored baseline still describes the page as it was before the change, so the identical drift would be reported again on the very next check. Note what accepting says: that the new page is the right one. A page that genuinely rotted would be marked healthy, which is why there is no "accept everything" and the rows are always ones you picked.
config.helpHealthMaintenanceBody:
A self-hosted service that takes itself down for ten minutes every night — a backup, a restart, a certificate renewal — is not broken. Left alone, a monitor cannot tell the difference: every one of those ten-minute gaps becomes an incident, an alert, and a dent in the uptime percentage, night after night, until the alerts stop meaning anything.

Config → Behavior → Status & health → Maintenance windows fixes the timing rather than the symptom. Add a window with a day, a start time and an end time — Sunday 02:00–02:30, say, for a weekly job. A window whose end is earlier than its start is read as running past midnight, since that is when most maintenance happens; there is no need for two windows either side of the hour. Windows are global, not per bookmark: they describe when you expect downtime, and every monitor is judged against that same clock.

Inside a window, checks still run exactly as normal and the heartbeat still records what happened — nothing is skipped or hidden. What changes is what a failure inside that window counts as: it does not open an incident, does not appear in the outage list, does not lower the uptime percentage, and does not trigger a webhook or push alert. A real outage that happens to start during the window is not swallowed either — the checks that keep failing after the window closes still raise the alarm in the normal way, because by then the failure has outlasted the excuse.
config.helpHealthWalkthroughTitle: Setting up one monitored bookmark, start to finish
config.helpHealthWalkthroughBody:
The settings above make more sense together than apart. Here is all of them, on one bookmark, in the order you would actually reach for them — a self-hosted status page at https://status.example.com, sitting behind a login and backed up every night at 3am.

1. Turn on Monitor. Right-click the bookmark, or open its editor, and set availability checking to Monitor rather than Periodic. This is your own server, checked whether or not the dashboard is open, and it is worth the small ongoing cost of a scheduled check for that reason alone — a bookmark to somebody else's blog would not usually earn the same treatment.

2. Pick an interval. Open the availability popover again and a Check interval row has appeared, because the bookmark is monitored now. A status page people rely on deserves closer watching than a personal blog, so 5 minutes makes sense here — the interval also decides how far back its heartbeat bar and history reach, so a 5-minute monitor reads as the last few hours rather than the last few weeks a slower one would show.

3. Tell it what "up" means for this page. The status page sits behind a login, so it always answers 401 when the check has no session — normal, not a failure. Type 200,401 into Status codes that count as healthy so a real outage (a 500, or no answer at all) is not lost in the noise of an expected 401. If the page also has a phrase that only appears when the underlying service it reports on is actually healthy — "All systems operational", say — put that in Text the page must contain too: a page that loads fine but is quietly reporting an incident of its own is a more specific, more useful thing to know than "the server answered".

4. Watch for the page changing shape entirely. Tick Watch for redirects, retitling and rewrites. This status page is one you built and pointed a domain at — if that domain's registration lapses, or a reverse-proxy config quietly starts sending it somewhere else, the keyword and status-code rules above would not catch it, because the request might never reach the real page at all. Drift watches for exactly that: a different host, a title that stops looking like your status page, a body that no longer matches what was saved.

5. Account for the backup window. The service restarts nightly at 3am for its backup, so under Config → Behavior → Status & health → Maintenance windows, add a window for every day, 03:00–03:10. Without it, this one monitor alone would raise an incident and an alert every single night — and after a week of that, a real 3am outage would read exactly like the six before it that meant nothing.

6. Wire up an alert. Under Downtime alerts, pick the service the team already watches — Slack for a shared channel, Pushover for a phone that should buzz even overnight, whichever fits. Set Alert after to 3 failures in a row, so one dropped check during a network blip does not page anyone, but three in a row — fifteen minutes of real downtime at this interval — does. Click Send test alert once and confirm the message actually lands where it is supposed to, before trusting it to carry the real one.

From here the bookmark looks after itself: its row grows a heartbeat bar and an uptime percentage, the Monitored filter's fleet panel folds it into the pooled numbers for everything else being watched, and a failure that is not inside the maintenance window and has failed three times running reaches Slack or Pushover within minutes — with a drift badge instead, if the page is still answering but is no longer the page anyone meant to be watching.
config.helpInboxBody:
The inbox (Shift + I, 0, or :inbox) is a holding area for links you want to keep without deciding where they go yet. Paste a URL onto the dashboard and, depending on your setting under Behavior → Inbox, it is added as a bookmark, dropped into the inbox, or you are asked which. A URL already sitting in the inbox is turned away rather than duplicated: the save is refused, a toast says Already in Inbox, and the dashboard jumps straight to the existing row instead of leaving you to go looking for it.

The browser extension's save popup has a Save to Inbox button alongside the normal page-and-category picker, so capturing a link never has to interrupt whatever you were doing to decide where it belongs. Whatever title and note you typed in the popup travel with it, the entry is tagged as having come from the extension, and the popup shows its own confirmation — including its own already saved message and a link that opens the inbox directly in nextDash — so you know the save landed before you close the tab.

New links stay unread until you open one or keep it with r or Space, and the header icon shows how many are waiting: it pulses and pops on every new arrival until the first time you actually open the inbox, after which it settles down to a plain, silent count — the animation is there to be noticed once, not to keep demanding attention afterward. Read links stay in the list — having read something is not a reason to remove it — until you clear them. Each link can be opened, promoted into a real bookmark, given a note (n) recording why you saved it, or deleted with undo.

A note is plain text, not markdown, with no length limit enforced — it is stored and shown exactly as typed, safely escaped, on the row and in triage cards. Editing one opens a small modal (or a browser prompt, if the modal cannot be shown) with the current note pre-filled.

Promoting opens the full bookmark form pre-filled, with every page and category to choose from — the inbox itself never assigns a page, category or tag to a link on its own, that choice is made once, at promote time. The inbox entry goes once the bookmark is saved, so nothing ends up filed in two places.

The ℹ at the end of the toolbar explains the same things from inside the view, and a sentence under the toolbar says what the filter you are on is showing.
config.helpInboxWorkBody:
Filter All, Unread, Snoozed or With note, narrow to a single site, and search. Each filter shows how many links are under it. Sorting offers newest first, oldest first, title or site — oldest first is how a backlog actually gets cleared, because the links you have been avoiding are at the bottom.

Snoozing (z) hides a link until a time you pick: three hours, tomorrow, the weekend, next week, or a date of your own. A snoozed link is left out of every count, tile and filter except Snoozed — so the numbers above the list always describe what is actually waiting for you — and comes back on its own once the time passes. Wake now brings one back early, and Clear read leaves snoozed links alone.

The list itself takes a keyboard without needing triage mode: j/k or the arrow keys move the selection, g and G (or Home and End) jump to the first and last row, x toggles a row's checkbox, and Escape clears the selection. Tick rows this way, or with the mouse, to mark read, snooze or delete just those — and export the filtered list, not the whole inbox, as CSV or JSON.

Filter, sort, search and site all appear in the address bar, so a view can be bookmarked or shared, and your filter, sort and chosen site come back on your next visit. A site filter is dropped once its last link leaves the inbox, rather than leaving you with an empty list.

Every number here counts the rows you can see: a search or a site filter narrows the tiles, the pills and the badge with the list. The site picker offers only the sites the active filter can reach and says how many rows each one leaves, and Mark all read becomes Mark shown read while something is narrowing the view. A line under the list says how many links are asleep and leads to them.

Import, beside the two export buttons, reads a JSON export back in — from another install, or edited by hand. Links already here are skipped rather than duplicated, and the message afterwards accounts for every row in the file.

A read link can go back to unread — right-click the row and pick Mark unread. The server always accepted it and no client ever sent it, so unread was the one inbox state that went one way only. The page description the server fetches when a link is captured is shown under the title too, and carried into both exports; the search matches it.
config.helpInboxTriageBody:
Triage is a different way of working the backlog: instead of scanning a list and clicking around it, one link is on screen at a time, full keyboard, no mouse needed. Start it from the Triage button, the t key while the inbox list has focus, or :inbox triage from anywhere.

j/k or the arrow keys move to the next or previous link, o or Enter opens the current one, p promotes it to a bookmark, r or Space keeps it and marks it read, and d or Delete removes it — each action lands and advances in one keystroke, so clearing a real backlog is a rhythm rather than a list of separate decisions. Escape closes triage and drops you back in the regular list, wherever you left off.

Triage reads from whatever filter and sort you had set before starting it, so running it from Unread, sorted oldest first, means you work the actual backlog in the order you have been avoiding it — while All or With note turn it into a quick way to skim links you already know about.
config.helpInboxSettingsBody:
Config → Behavior → Inbox has one switch that matters most: Enable the inbox. Turn it off and the inbox disappears from the page tabs, its keyboard shortcuts and command stop working, and a pasted URL is added straight as a bookmark — there is no in-between state to fall into by accident.

A couple of settings shape the inbox without a control in that screen at all — they only exist in the underlying settings file, for anyone who wants to reach for them directly:

  • A cap on how many links it holds (500 by default). Crossing it does not warn you or archive the overflow: the oldest entries are silently dropped to make room for new ones, newest first. An inbox that is otherwise left to grow forever is, in practice, one that quietly loses its tail — a reason on its own to work it down with Triage rather than let it become a permanent queue.
  • Deduplicating by URL, on by default, which is what makes pasting the same link twice a no-op rather than a second row.

Both take effect the moment they are changed in the file — nothing needs restarting, and neither has any bearing on bookmarks already promoted out of the inbox, since those are ordinary bookmarks from that point on.

At the cap, undo still works. Undoing a delete puts the link back with the time it was originally saved, not the time you pressed undo — which, in a full inbox, is exactly the item the cap would otherwise drop. A returning link is therefore kept and the oldest of the others makes way for it. If there is genuinely no room, the undo says the inbox is full rather than reporting success and quietly discarding the link, which is what would leave it looking restored until the next reload.
config.helpInboxTourBody:
The first time you open the inbox, a short guided tour walks the whole loop in seven steps: where links come from, what read really means, snoozing, notes, promoting, triage, and selection. It appears once — finishing it, skipping it or pressing Escape all count as seen, so it never interrupts twice.

Everything it covers is documented on this page in more depth, and the ℹ in the inbox toolbar gives the short version whenever you want it. Turning off Show occasional keyboard tips under Behavior → General → Onboarding stops the tour, and every other one-time hint, from appearing at all. Show quick-start card again, in the same place, brings it back once you have seen it.
config.helpDataBody:
Data & backups is where your data goes in and out.

Backups snapshot everything — bookmarks, pages, categories, finders, your inbox, settings, themes, and the uptime history of monitored bookmarks. Restoring replaces what is there — nextDash writes a copy of the current data first, on the server, so a restore you regret is itself undoable. An archive with no bookmark file in it is refused rather than applied: committing an import removes the pages the archive does not name, so a file like that used to empty the library and report success. You can create a backup on demand, restore any stored one, or download it as a file.

Automatic backups keep a safety net without you remembering: nextDash writes a full backup on a schedule — weekly unless you pick daily, fortnightly or monthly under How often — and keeps the newest three, dropping the oldest as new ones arrive. The panel says as much beside the list, because making a backup on a full rotation removes one. NEXTDASH_AUTO_BACKUP_KEEP raises that count and NEXTDASH_AUTO_BACKUP_DIR moves the archives off the data directory altogether. Each is listed with its age, size and what is inside it — 1.7 MB · 412 bookmarks on 5 pages — with the exact moment in its tooltip, and Download, Restore and Delete beside it. Download all saves the lot. If you run in Docker, keep the data directory on a mounted volume so these survive a rebuild.

Import and export. Import an HTML bookmark file exported from a browser and its folders become categories, with duplicates skipped. Export yours the same way to move elsewhere, or take a full archive of everything at once. :backup and :export reach both from the dashboard. A CSV export can also be read back in, so you can tidy hundreds of rows in a spreadsheet — fixing categories, adding tags — and return the result; unlike the browser file, that route carries tags and notes.

Trash catches deleted bookmarks, pages and categories, and holds them for 30 days before they go for good. The toast's undo is for the moment right after; the trash is for the next morning. Restore puts a bookmark back on its own page at the position it had. A deleted page is kept as a single entry — shown as Page · 12 bookmarks — and restoring brings the page, its categories and its bookmarks back together, at its original place in the tab strip. Every delete goes through it — from the dashboard, from the health view, and from Config → Bookmarks, singly or twenty at a time. Delete forever or Empty trash clear it early. A restore that cannot go ahead is refused rather than forced, and the item stays in the trash: a category whose page is gone needs that page back first, and a page whose old slot has since been taken by another page cannot replace it. A search box narrows the list by name, address, tag, category or the page it came from, and several rows can be ticked and restored in one go — each on its own, so one that cannot come back does not stop the rest.

The housekeeping has tabs of its own. Icons & previews refreshes favicons and clears cached link previews, Server log shows what the server has been doing, and Reset holds the ways to start over. Reset asks for confirmation, and a backup beforehand is worth the few seconds.

The server log says what it is doing, and how much of it. Every line names its level and the part of the server it came from — WARN archive dash.example could not be saved: the page is behind a login — written for whoever runs nextDash rather than for whoever wrote it. Detail level decides how much is written at all, here and in docker logs alike: Quiet for problems only, Normal for what the server did, Verbose for every step. It acts on the next line, with no restart. That is a different question from Show, which only narrows what you are looking at — a note under it says which level is recording, so “why do I see nothing” has one answer instead of two guesses. Activity trail beside it picks what goes into the machine-readable record: changes and check results to begin with, and nine more channels — health rounds, imports, feed polls, saved copies, backups, failed writes, widget requests, alerts sent, bookmarks opened — off until you ask for them.

Your data lives as plain JSON files in one directory on the server, so backing up that directory backs up everything, and open dashboard tabs notice when another tab saves and refresh themselves.

The trash is a command away. :trash from the dashboard opens Data & backups → Trash, where deleted bookmarks, pages and categories wait 30 days. It used to be reachable by mouse only — the toast’s undo is for the moment right after, and the trash is for the next morning, when you are on the dashboard.

A failed automatic backup says so. The outcome of the last scheduled attempt is shown on the Last backup tile, which turns red and names the error. A failing run only wrote a log line before, so a full disk could stop backups for months while the panel looked normal — the newest file’s date does not move when a run fails.
config.helpSourcesBody:
An import reads a file once. A source is a place bookmarks keep arriving from, and is asked again. They have their own tab, Data & backups → Sources, rather than sitting beside the import buttons — two things called import on neighbouring tabs is a question you would have to answer before every click.

Five to start with. GitHub stars and Raindrop.io need a token. Hacker News, YouTube and Mastodon need nothing at all: all three publish public XML at a predictable address, so a username or a channel is the whole setup.

Every source answers the same four questions — what is my token, where should its bookmarks land, import now, and what happened last time. Each one previews what it would write before writing it, so a first run cannot surprise you, and each remembers where it got to, so a second run brings only what is new. The Sources widget puts the last result of every source on your dashboard, which is where a failed import becomes visible without going looking for it.

The browser bookmark file is on the neighbouring tab, under Backups & data. It is the thirty-year-old format every browser exports, and that Pocket, Pinboard, Raindrop, linkding, Shiori, Linkwarden and Karakeep all speak: folders become categories, and tags, notes and the date you saved a link travel with it. Export bookmarks (HTML) hands your collection back in the same format.

Tokens live in a file of their own in your data directory, readable only by the account nextDash runs as, and stay out of your backups unless you switch stored tokens on under What a backup carries.
config.helpArchiveTitle: Keeping a copy of a page
config.helpArchiveBody:
The health view tells you a link is dead. This is the other half — having a copy when it happens. All three settings live under Data & backups → Sources.

The Web Archive, on the day you save. Switch on Archive new bookmarks and a copy is requested the day a bookmark is added, rather than hoping somebody else captured it before it died — for a page nobody else bookmarked, usually nobody did. Without an archive.org key pair the archive still accepts captures, but at a far smaller daily allowance, so the panel takes an access key and a secret and has a button that captures one page so you can prove them. A capture is queued rather than instant; the panel says what became of it, including the refusal that looks like success, since a sixth capture of the same page in one day comes back as an ordinary success.

A copy on your own disk. Local copies saves a whole page — text, styling and images — as a single file in your data directory. It asks nobody's permission and stays readable when both the site and the Web Archive are gone. Bookmarks → Local copies lists what you have, grouped by the bookmark it belongs to, since the question is almost always what do I have of this page; copies whose bookmark has since been deleted get a group of their own rather than vanishing with it.

archive.today, as a second opinion. The two archives disagree by design: the Web Archive honours a site that turns it away and drops what a site later withdraws, while archive.today keeps what it captured. For a link that died behind a paywall or a takedown, no copy from the first is routinely not no copy.

The date the web lost a page. The health view reads the archive's own index rather than asking for the capture nearest to now — that one answers about any capture, including one that archived an error page, which for a dead link is usually exactly what comes back.
config.helpIntegrationsBody:
Everything nextDash talks to, it talks to on its own schedule: it polls a feed, checks a host, fetches an icon. Nothing outside could find out that something happened here without asking. Two things on Data & backups → Webhooks change that, and both start switched off.

Outgoing webhooks. Give a receiver a name and an address, tick which events it should hear about, and save. Five events: a bookmark added, changed or removed, and a monitored bookmark going down or coming back. Nothing ticked means everything.

Every delivery is signed, using a published scheme rather than one of our own, so a receiver that already verifies those needs no special case. An endpoint listening for a bookmark was added is a URL anyone who learns it can post to, and a receiver acting on an unsigned request acts on whatever the internet tells it. The signing key is shown once, in the answer to the save that generated it — copy it into the receiver then; afterwards the screen only says a key is set.

A failed delivery is retried twice with a growing gap and then given up on. A refusal from the receiver is not retried at all: that is it saying the request itself is wrong, and sending it again unchanged gets the same answer while looking like an outage. Send a test posts one delivery and reports what came back.

An assistant that speaks MCP can search your bookmarks, look one up, list your tags and add a new one — without being told about an API in a prompt that then goes stale. Tick Answer assistants at this address and the panel shows the address to paste into the assistant. It starts closed because it answers questions about every bookmark in the install, which is not something to add to a default install quietly; and if you run with a write token, an assistant needs it to write.
config.helpWidgetsBody:
A page holds categories of bookmarks. Since 1.4.0 it can also hold widgets: blocks that show something other than links, drawn among your categories, dragged into place the same way and stored in the same order. There is one list arranging a page, not two.

They read what nextDash already keeps. Nothing here polls anything new: the health report, the sample history, the inbox store, the feed and source registers and your own last opened timestamps are all on disk already, and had nowhere to show. A figure on a tile is a link into the rows behind it — click the broken count and you land on those bookmarks, filtered.

One column or two. Two is the maximum, and it reuses the span rule a wide category already has rather than growing a second way to be wide; on a single-column dashboard a wide widget narrows itself again. A widget is a summary, and one that needs three columns is a view that has not admitted it yet.

A tile says what it left out. Six of them cut their list to a chosen row count, and a silent cut is a lie: five of twelve looked exactly like five of five. The row count is your choice about what you want to see, so what falls outside it stays visible as a number.

A widget folds away. Click its title — or press Enter or Space with the header focused — and the block folds shut, the same gesture the categories beside it have always had. Fold all and the . key take widgets with them, and each block stays as you left it, per page.

The custom widget keeps itself up to date. It is the one tile that reads a service of your own rather than something nextDash already keeps — and until 1.4.2.1 the only way to see a newer figure was to reload the page, so a dashboard left open all day showed the download speed it found at breakfast. Each custom tile now refreshes on the interval in its own settings: 60 seconds for a download speed, five minutes for a queue, an hour for something measured hourly. The presets already carry a sensible figure per service, so there is nothing to set. While the tab is in the background nothing is asked at all, so a dashboard on a second monitor does not spend the day questioning your own machines. Right-click its title for Refresh now when you have just fixed something and do not want to wait for the next beat, and the interval field says what it accepts — between 30 seconds and 24 hours — with an ℹ beside it explaining how to choose.
config.helpSelfHostingBody:
nextDash is self-hosted: it runs as a single binary or container, stores everything in plain JSON files in one data directory, and needs no database. Point the container at a volume and upgrades are just a new image.

Because the data is plain files, you can read or edit it with ordinary tools, and backing up that one directory is a complete backup.

Production Docker. Use docker-compose.prod.yml for deployments: only ./data is mounted and static assets ship inside the Go binary (embed). Since v2026.08.02 the image is smaller (~40% less), runs as non-root user nextdash, and the compose file sets a 256 MB memory cap. For TLS and long-cache static serving in front of the app, see docker-compose.proxy.yml with deploy/Caddyfile. Use docker-compose.yml for development when you mount ./static and ./templates for live edits.

Access. There is no account system: anyone who can reach the URL can read and write unless you put something in front of it. Keep it on your own network, or behind whatever authentication your reverse proxy or tunnel provides, and do not expose plain HTTP to the internet. A write token can be required for write APIs, which the dashboard supplies automatically once you are using it in a browser. The data directory itself is not published: only data/icons/ and a favicon or font you uploaded are served over HTTP, so settings, bookmark files, the inbox, the trash and stored backups are reachable only through the API that token guards.

There is no telemetry beyond the optional, off-by-default usage analytics under Behavior → Privacy.

The browser extension saves the current tab to nextDash, with an optional shortcut, tags, and notes, and can save to the inbox instead of picking a page. It needs your server URL, and the write token if you set one.

If something looks wrong. Bookmarks that seem to have vanished are almost always a page or category filter still applied in the Bookmarks list rather than lost data. Sorting surprises usually mean a category is on A–Z or Recent, or a pinned bookmark is doing its job. Search that misses something is often a filter token like tag: still in the box. The README on GitHub covers the compose file, environment variables, and upgrade notes.
config.helpAboutBody:
nextDash is a self-hosted, keyboard-first bookmark dashboard: fast to search, quick to organise, and yours to host. No accounts, no tracking, no database — just your bookmarks in plain files on a server you control.

Two tabs here. This one is the colophon; News & features beside it carries the full news stream — every post from nextdash.cc, every release, and every setting worth switching on, including the ones from releases before the catalogue was dated — with the same source filters the overview uses. At the foot of it, one button saves nextdash.cc as a bookmark so Fresh counts its posts for you, which is also the shortest demonstration of what Fresh is for.

nextdash.cc is the project's own site: what it does, screenshots, and how to get it running. Its feed is what the overview reads. jordibrw.nl is where the person behind it writes. Issues, feature requests and release notes live on GitHub, and if nextDash saves you time, the Ko-fi link below is the way to say thanks.
config.settingsSearchPromoBody: Find any setting, tab, or help section from here. Type a keyword and pick a result — or press <kbd>Ctrl+Shift+K</kbd> (<kbd>Cmd+Shift+K</kbd> on Mac). <kbd>Ctrl+K</kbd> opens quick actions only.
config.helpVersionBody:
This is version 1.4.4, and it is mostly about themes. There are 214 of them and they arrived through a list; there is a browser now — a searchable grid of cards, one per family, with favourites, and the dashboard offers to open it for you once. Every theme has been given its own accent instead of borrowing the success colour, a depth setting that lets a card sit on a surface rather than beside a border, an improved backdrop you can set to dots, grid, lines or hatch, and thirty-three new families have joined them. Alongside that: a page can hold widgets, now with twenty-eight services the custom tile already knows; Statistics reports uptime, expiring certificates and how much of your collection has a saved copy; Sources keeps bookmarks arriving on their own; a page can be kept at the Web Archive or on your own disk; webhooks and an MCP endpoint tell the rest of your machine what happened here; and your browser's address bar is a nextDash search box.

1.4.4 is the newest round, and it is about who can read it: Chinese joins as a fifth full language — 简体中文 across the dashboard, config, statistics, health and all 209 headings of this tab, with nothing falling back to English on the way through. The theme browser, which had stayed English in every language, was translated with it. Alongside that, search results group by why they matched — the strong ones stay open, the rest fold behind a heading and a count — and the ranking learns, reading how often you open a bookmark and remembering which result you chose for the keystrokes you chose it with. Six fixes travel with them, the loudest being a Periodic switch that saved your change without saying so.
config.bookmarkDashboardPreviewHint: Hover to see the full tile
config.bookmarkLinkPreviewEmpty: No preview metadata yet — refresh to fetch title, description and image.
config.bookmarkPreviewMaintenanceHint: Refresh or clear title, description and image stored on bookmarks for hover cards and tooltips on the dashboard.

config.categoriesIntro:
Categories organise bookmarks within a page. Select a page to manage its categories.
Drag the ⠿ handle to reorder (saves automatically). Merge combines two categories and moves their bookmarks. On the Bookmarks tab, the Context panel only switches the active category filter.
config.collectionsEmptyHint: No collections yet. Create one to group bookmarks by tag, category, or shortcut.
config.categoriesListEmptyHint: No categories on this page yet. Add one to organise bookmarks.
config.categoriesMobileOnlyDesktop: Category management is available on desktop. Open config on a larger screen to add or reorder categories.
config.categoryNameMustBeUnique: Category name must be unique and not empty.
config.collectionStatsEmpty: No collections are active right now.
config.findersIntro: A finder is a shortcut to a search engine. Set a search URL with %s where your query should go (e.g. https://www.google.com/search?q=%s), pick a short letter shortcut, and on the dashboard type ? plus that shortcut and your words — e.g. ?du linux opens DuckDuckGo with “linux” in your browser.
config.pagesIntro:
Pages group your bookmarks. Each page has its own set of categories and bookmarks on the dashboard.
Drag the ⠿ handle to reorder pages (saves automatically). Use Archive to hide a page without deleting its bookmarks. Double-click a page tab on the dashboard to rename it, set an emoji, and pick a colour dot. On the Bookmarks tab, the Context panel only switches the active page.
config.dashboardSyncFailed: Dashboard sync failed. Retry from config.
config.tagsTabIntro: Manage tags across all bookmarks. Rename or delete tags globally, or see which bookmarks carry each tag. Changes save automatically.
config.tagsListEmptyHint: No tags yet. Add tags to bookmarks via the Bookmarks tab or the inline editor on the dashboard.
config.tagsMobileOnlyDesktop: Tag management is available on desktop. Open config on a larger screen to rename, merge, or delete tags.
config.tagMergeMessage: Tag "{new}" already exists on {count} bookmarks. Merge "{old}" into it?
config.tagDeleteMessage: Removes the tag from {count} bookmarks. Bookmarks are kept.
config.themeInfoMessage:
Chooses the colour theme for the dashboard and config.

• Includes built-in dark/light and any custom themes from Config → theme
• Saved when you click Save in config
config.autoDarkModeInfoMessage:
Automatically switches between light and dark theme based on your system preference.

• Only works with built-in themes that have dark and light variants
• Not available with custom themes — those use one fixed palette
• Useful on laptops and phones that follow OS appearance
config.randomThemeModeInfoMessage:
Picks a different theme from the pool instead of your saved choice.

• Off — always use the theme selected above
• On page refresh — new random theme on each reload (F5)
• On view change — new random theme when switching between bookmarks, config, inbox, and health, or when switching between dashboard pages

With auto dark mode on, only dark or light variants matching your system appearance are chosen. Custom themes without a dark/light pair are skipped when auto dark mode is on.

If random is on and you pick a different saved theme, your choice is stored but the display keeps rotating until you turn random off — a toast confirms this.
config.randomThemeChoiceSavedHint: Random theme is on — your choice is saved, but the display keeps picking from the pool until you turn random off.

config.systemAppearanceHintIdle: Your OS appearance right now. Enable auto dark mode to switch themes when this changes.
config.systemAppearanceHintUnsupported: System appearance shown for reference. Auto dark mode needs a built-in dark/light theme pair — not available with custom themes.
config.backgroundPickerInfoMessage:
Optional wallpaper behind the bookmark grid.

• None: plain theme background
• Auto: gradient matched to the active theme
• Gradient / Image: pick a preset or paste an image URL
• Opacity slider controls how strong it appears
config.backgroundOpacityInfoMessage:
How visible the background is (65–100%).

• Lower values keep bookmarks easier to read
• Applies to gradient and image backgrounds
config.enableAnimationsInfoMessage:
UI transitions and motion effects.

• On: smoother category collapse, modals, etc.
• Off: snappier feel, can help on slower devices
config.fontPresetInfoMessage:
Font family for the whole interface.

• Mono fonts suit the terminal aesthetic
• Sans fonts are easier for long reading

config.fontWeightInfoMessage:
How bold body text appears.

config.iconStylingInfoMessage:
Tints bookmark favicons to match the active theme.

config.columnsInfoMessage:
How many bookmark tiles fit on one row (1–6).

config.layoutVersionInfoMessage:
Switch between classic and modern dashboard styling.

Modern is not finished yet. Use Classic for the best experience.

config.layoutPresetInfoMessage:
Overall bookmark grid style.

config.densityModeInfoMessage:

config.showDashboardTitleInfoMessage:
Shows the nextDash title (or custom title) at the top.

• Off: more vertical space for bookmarks
config.launcherIconSizeInfoMessage:
Icon scale when using the Launcher layout preset.

• Only applies in Launcher mode
config.calendarUrlInfoMessage:
Link opened when you use the calendar shortcut from the date line.

config.showIconsInfoMessage:
Shows favicons on each bookmark.

• Fetched automatically when adding links
• Can be refreshed from config → data & backups
config.showShortcutsInfoMessage:
Where a bookmark's keyboard shortcut appears on its row.

• Never — no letters; the shortcuts themselves keep working
config.showPinIconInfoMessage:
Small pin marker on pinned bookmarks.

• Pin via command :pin or inline edit
config.showNoteIconInfoMessage:
Indicator when a bookmark has a note.

• Notes are edited with :note or inline edit
config.showLinkPreviewCardsInfoMessage:
Hover card with title/description preview for a bookmark.

• Only on keyboard focus or hover
• Delay setting avoids accidental popups
config.linkPreviewHoverDelayInfoMessage:
How long to wait before showing the preview card.

• Fast (100ms), Balanced (150ms), Calm (250ms — the default)
config.openLinksInNewTabInfoMessage:
Opens bookmark URLs in a new browser tab.

• Off: replaces the current tab
• HyprMode (Advanced) changes PWA behavior
config.pasteUrlQuickAddInfoMessage:
Paste a URL on the dashboard to open the new-bookmark flow.

• Works when no input field is focused
• Ctrl+V on dashboard
config.languageInfoMessage:
Interface language for dashboard, config, and modals.

• Applies immediately in config

config.showDateInfoMessage:
Date line in the dashboard header.

config.dateFormatInfoMessage:
How the date is formatted.

config.showTimeInfoMessage:
Clock in the dashboard header.

config.showWeatherWithDateInfoMessage:
Shows temperature (and conditions when available) beside the date.

How location is determined.

config.weatherLocationInfoMessage:
City or place name for manual weather lookup.

How often nextDash fetches new weather data.

config.buttonBarPositionInfoMessage:

config.showDockLayoutSelectorInfoMessage:
Shows a layout switcher in the footer dock.

config.colorizeStatusInfoMessage:
Highlights offline bookmarks with a red row.

config.showPingTimesInfoMessage:
Displays response time in milliseconds next to status.

• Only when status checks are enabled
config.showStatusLoadingInfoMessage:
Spinner or loading state while a status check runs.

• Helps on slow networks
config.deviceSpecificSettingsInfoMessage:
Stores certain preferences per browser/device instead of globally.

config.enableCustomFaviconInfoMessage:
Upload an icon shown in the browser tab for nextDash.

config.enableCustomTitleInfoMessage:
Replaces the default nextDash title in the tab bar.

config.showPageInTitleInfoMessage:
Appends the active page name to the browser tab title.

config.fuzzySuggestionsStartWithInfoMessage:
When fuzzy suggestions are on, only show matches that start with your query.

config.configGeneralTourWelcomeBody: This page controls how your dashboard looks and behaves. Changes apply after you click Save — the dashboard updates without a full reload.
config.configGeneralTourLayersBody: Everyday options live under Essentials. Power features (smart collections, status checks, branding, search behavior) are under Advanced. Choose All sections for one scrollable page — Expand all / Collapse all appear in the toolbar.
config.configGeneralTourAppearanceBody: Theme, font size, animations, and rotating tips. Use the ℹ buttons for details on any setting.
config.configGeneralTourLayoutBody: Choose Classic or Modern styling, then pick a layout preset and density. On the dashboard, switch quickly with :LAYOUTVERSION or :LAYOUTVERSION toggle. Themes still control all colors in both versions.
config.configGeneralTourBookmarksBody: How bookmarks are sorted, whether icons and shortcuts show, and whether links open in a new tab. Clipboard prompts and page tabs are here too.
config.configGeneralTourToolbarBody: Choose which buttons appear in the footer: search, finders, commands, recent bookmarks, health, and more.
config.configGeneralTourSmartBody: Turn automatic groups like Today or Most used on or off. Open Advanced → Smart for limits, keywords, and per-collection tuning.
config.configGeneralTourAdvancedBody: Jump to appearance fine-tuning, bookmark display, live status pings, custom title/favicon, search overlay behavior, and system tools. Date, time, and weather live under Localization in this view.
config.configGeneralTourTabsBody: Pages, categories, bookmarks, finders, collections, and backups are managed on their own tabs. Theme colors have a dedicated editor under theme.
config.configGeneralTourSaveBody: Click Save when you are done. Unsaved changes are highlighted; Discard reverts to the last saved state.
config.languageAppliesImmediately: Language changes apply immediately (no Save needed).
config.resetExpandToConfirm: Expand this section to access the reset button.
config.configGeneralTourSearchBody: Use the search box to jump to a setting on any tab. Matching sections expand automatically so the control is visible.

config.finderUrlMissingPlaceholderHint: Add %s where the search query should go.

config.tipConfigKeyboard: In config: j/k move sections or the bookmark list, 0–9 leave for Inbox or a page, and Ctrl+Shift+K finds any setting — press ! for the full cheat sheet. Shift+S returns where you left off.
config.tipConfigFindValue: Ctrl+Shift+K also matches what a setting is set to — search 8099 or Monitor when you know the value but not the name.
config.tipEverydayModes: Type > to search, : for commands, ? for finders — all from the keyboard, no clicking.
config.tipEverydayPages: 1–9 jumps straight to a page; Shift+←/→ steps through them.
config.tipEverydayArrows: ↑↓←→ moves between bookmarks, Enter opens the selected one.
config.tipEverydayEsc: Esc always backs out of whatever is open.
config.tipEverydayOverview: , shows every page with its bookmark count.
config.tipEverydayViews: Shift+H opens health, Shift+I the inbox, and Shift+S config — the header icons use the same keys.
config.tipEverydayGridFilter: Shift+F narrows the page you are on in place, keeping the layout and the cursor — where > searches everywhere.
config.tipEverydayScrollBack: A long page remembers where you were: switch pages, open health or config, come back, and you land at the offset you left.
config.tipEverydayCheatsheet: ! or F1 opens the full keyboard cheat sheet — every shortcut in one place.
config.tipAddPaste: Paste a URL anywhere on the dashboard and the new-bookmark modal opens pre-filled.
config.tipAddQuickAdd: & is the fastest way in: type name | url | shortcut in one field.
config.tipAddFullModal: + or Shift+B opens the full modal when you need page, category, tags and preview.
config.tipAddShortcut: Give a bookmark a shortcut and you can open it by typing that shortcut and pressing Enter. Typing never opens anything on its own, so a word like invoice stays a search.
config.tipEditInline: Shift+E edits the selected bookmark inline — no dialog, no page change.
config.tipEditQuickActions: Shift+M moves it, Shift+T tags it, Shift+D deletes it. Each opens a small popover.
config.tipEditUndo: Deleted the wrong one? The toast has an Undo for a few seconds.
config.tipEditDrag: Drag the strip on the left of a row to reorder; drag the // in a category header to reorder categories.
config.tipEditMoveCategory: Shift+Alt+← / → moves the selected bookmark into the category beside it; Alt alone moves the category itself.
config.tipEditSelectionActions: Tick several rows and the toolbar can pin them, set their checking mode, and undo a tag change in one step — a mixed selection pins rather than flipping each row.
config.tipEditRenamePage: Double-click a page tab to rename it and give it an emoji and colour.
config.tipEditPageTabDot: Double-click a page tab and pick a colour swatch — a colour dot appears on the tab so you can tell pages apart at a glance.
config.tipFindAddressBar: Your browser's address bar is a nextDash search box: after one visit, type the keyword, Tab, a term, Enter. Give it a short keyword in the browser's own settings.
config.tipTuneWidgets: A page can hold widgets as well as categories — uptime, a thirty-day trend, the inbox, what you never opened, and the sources, feeds and certificates that need attention. Config → Widgets, then drag them into place.
config.tipTuneWidgetFold: A widget folds away like a category: click its title, or press Enter with the header focused. . folds every block on the page, widgets included.
config.tipTuneCustomWidget: Service not in the widget list? The custom widget points at any address that answers with JSON and draws the fields you name. It is fetched by the server, so a local address works and no key reaches your browser.
config.tipMaintSignIn: A self-hosted service that answers not signed in reads as broken. Store the sign-in once under Data & backups → Sources → Health sign-ins and point any number of bookmarks at it.
config.tipMaintArchive: Switch on Archive new bookmarks and a copy is requested the day you save a link — the health view can then offer a copy of the page rather than only telling you it is gone. Local copies keeps one on your own disk.
config.tipDataSources: Data & backups → Sources keeps bookmarks arriving from GitHub stars, Raindrop.io, Hacker News, YouTube and Mastodon. The last three need no token — a username or a channel is the whole setup.
config.tipDataWebhooks: Something else on your network can be told when a bookmark changes or a monitored link goes down: Data & backups → Webhooks. Every delivery is signed. The same tab opens nextDash to an AI assistant, off until you switch it on.
config.tipDataPortable: Bring a whole browser's bookmarks in — or any read-later tool's export — with Import bookmarks (HTML): folders become categories, and tags, notes and dates travel with them. Export bookmarks (HTML) hands your collection back in the same format.
config.tipFindFilters: Search narrows with tag:, category:, status: and page: — combine them with plain words.
config.tipFindShortcutMode: A bookmark shortcut opens the moment it matches. If an ordinary word of yours keeps getting swallowed, Behavior → Search offers after a pause and press Enter instead.
config.tipFindAllPages: Prefix a search with @ to look across every page instead of the current one.
config.tipFindFinders: Finders send your text to a search engine: ?g term googles it.
config.tipFindTagCloud: / opens the tag cloud — click a tag to filter the dashboard down to it.
config.tipFindRecent: * lists what you opened recently; :open last 5 reopens them in tabs.
config.tipMaintHealth: The health page finds broken links, duplicates and bookmarks you have not touched in a long time.
config.tipMaintReview: When enough links want attention, the dashboard offers a two-minute session over the worst ten — it ends with a count, and Done for today stops it coming back until tomorrow.
config.tipMaintRotReport: Rot report in the health toolbar adds it all up: what has gone, what has moved, what has been failing for over a month, and what broke this week.
config.tipMaintMerge: Duplicates can be merged from the health page in one bulk action.
config.tipMaintMonitorStats: Press i on a monitored bookmark in the health view to open its full statistics — uptime over 24 hours, 7 days and 30 days, a large response-time chart and every outage.
config.tipMaintCert: A certificate about to expire is invisible until it breaks. Monitored bookmarks on HTTPS warn you 30, 7 and 3 days ahead — the health view badges the rows and counts them in a Certificates tile.
config.tipMaintExpectText: A page can answer perfectly while showing “Database connection failed”. On a monitored row, set Expected response to a phrase that only appears when it works, and a broken page stops counting as up.
config.tipMaintMaintenanceWindow: Alerted every night by a backup that takes a host down for ten minutes? A maintenance window under Behavior → Status & health silences the expected downtime without hiding a real outage.
config.tipMaintTrash: Deleted something you wanted? Deleted bookmarks, pages and categories wait 30 days in config → data & backups → trash, long after the undo toast has gone.
config.tipMaintBackup: Back up everything — pages, bookmarks and settings — under config → data & backups. Restoring replaces what you have, so back up first.
config.tipMaintNote: :note edits a bookmark's note without leaving the dashboard.
config.tipTuneInfo: Every setting in config has an ℹ button explaining what it does.
config.tipTuneTheme: The dark/light button in the header flips the theme instantly, without touching config.
config.tipTunePreview: Link preview cards are off by default — turn them on under config → appearance → display, then hover a bookmark.
config.tipTuneSmartCollections: Smart collections fill themselves from rules; you never add bookmarks to them by hand.
config.tipTuneFresh: Switch on Fresh (Behavior → Status & health) and a bookmark whose page has a feed carries a small count of what it published since you last opened it.
config.tipTuneCommands: Commands like :favicons off or :dark change settings live, without a round trip to config.

config.tagsEmpty: No tags yet. Add tags to bookmarks to manage them here.

config.tipCategoryWidth: Spread the focused category across columns, or put it back
config.widgetsSectionIntro: Blocks on a page that hold something other than bookmarks — what is broken, what is waiting, what has gone quiet.
config.widgetGroupCustom: And anything else: the Custom widget
config.widgetsAddNote: Choose a kind and it lands at the end of the page. Everything about it is editable afterwards.
config.widgetsAddCustomNote: Reads a figure out of any service that answers JSON, and can start from one of the services already known. The Types tab explains what it can do.
config.widgetCustomRefLead: Every widget above reads something nextDash already knows. The Custom widget reads a figure out of any service that answers JSON, so a tile can show what your own machines are doing without waiting for nextDash to grow a widget for them.
config.widgetCustomRefAddressBody: Any http or https endpoint, fetched by the server rather than by the browser — so a service on your own network works, and no key ever reaches the page. GET, or POST with a body for the services that insist.
config.widgetCustomRefPathsBody: Name the value you want and nothing else — the path walks objects and arrays. Up to eight figures on one tile; more than that is a report rather than a glance.
config.widgetCustomRefFormatsBody: The same number reads differently depending on what it is:
config.widgetCustomRefListTitle: Or a list instead of figures
config.widgetCustomRefListBody: Point at an array and the tile draws its entries as rows, up to twenty — the downloads running now, the last few errors.
config.widgetCustomRefAuthTitle: A sign-in that stays out of your backups
config.widgetCustomRefAuthBody: An API key in a header, or a username and password. Kept in a separate file that no export or backup ZIP includes; the widget itself stores only a reference to it.
config.widgetCustomRefCacheTitle: Asked on a schedule you set
config.widgetCustomRefCacheBody: Anywhere between 30 seconds and a day, five minutes by default. One answer is shared by everyone looking at the dashboard, so a wall display costs the service nothing extra.
config.widgetCustomRefPresetsTitle: Or start from a service already known
config.widgetCustomRefPresetsBody: Filled in for you: the address, the figures worth reading, and the header its API wants. {count} services in four groups, and everything stays editable afterwards.
config.widgetCustomRefLimits: What it will not do is change anything. A tile reads, and the two methods it offers are the two that ask a question. An answer has eight seconds to arrive and is read up to a megabyte.
config.widgetTypesIntro: Every kind of widget nextDash can draw. Add one straight from this list.

config.buttonBarPositionDesc.bottom-left: Docked in the bottom-left corner, clear of the bookmarks.
config.buttonBarPositionDesc.bottom-right: Docked in the bottom-right corner, clear of the bookmarks — the default.
config.buttonBarPositionDesc.side-left: A vertical rail down the left edge, always in reach.
config.buttonBarPositionDesc.side-right: A vertical rail down the right edge, always in reach.

config.chromeGroupPrimaryNote: The four everyday actions. Hiding one leaves its keyboard shortcut working.
config.chromeGroupSecondaryNote: The second group, beside the main buttons. With all of these off the group disappears entirely.

config.shortcutDisplayHover: Only on the row you are on
config.shortcutDisplayHoverBody: The letters stay out of the way and the bookmark names get the width back. The shortcut appears when the pointer or the keyboard selection is on the row.
config.shortcutDisplayAlwaysBody: Every shortcut is on screen, in a column of its own down the right of each category. The names have that much less room.
config.shortcutDisplayNeverBody: No letters anywhere. The shortcuts themselves keep working.
