config.helpWidgetKindsTitle: The kinds, and what each answers
config.helpWidgetKindsBody:
Thirteen built-in kinds, grouped in the picker under the question they answer.

Are the links still good? Health — how many bookmarks are broken, down, changed or fine, each figure opening its own filter. Uptime — the bookmarks you monitor, worst first, with uptime over the last week. Certificates — certificates about to expire, grouped by host rather than by bookmark, because ten bookmarks on one domain share one certificate. Health trend — broken links over time as a line, because the direction is what a single number cannot show.

What is arriving? Inbox — how much is waiting to be filed, and how long the oldest has waited. Feeds — feeds with new items, and the ones that stopped after repeated failures. Sources — what each import last did, so a failed import is not only visible inside config.

What needs tidying? Neglected — bookmarks you have not opened in a long time. Blind spots — never checked, checked long ago, or not watched at all. Duplicates — the same address stored more than once. Archive — how many bookmarks have a copy kept, and which broken ones have none. Trash — what is waiting there, and when retention removes it. Backups — how old the newest automatic backup is, and whether the last run failed.

And a fourteenth that is not a report but a capability: the Custom widget, below.
config.helpWidgetAddingTitle: Adding one, and where it sits
config.helpWidgetAddingBody:
Config → Widgets opens on the widgets you have, with one Add a widget button above them. The catalogue opens over the page rather than filling it — it used to sit open at the top of the tab, which pushed your own widgets below the fold, so choosing a kind added something you could not see. Now it closes onto the new widget with its name ready to type.

The Types tab is the same catalogue as reading matter: every kind with what it does, and an Add button on each, so you can read about one and take it without changing screens.

Settings per widget. Which page it counts, how many rows it shows, what it is called, how wide it is. Leave the title empty and it uses the kind's own name. The Shown switch takes a widget off the dashboard without deleting it or losing its settings.

Where it sits is arranged under Pages & tags → categories, together with the categories it sits between — one order, one place to change it. On the dashboard you can also just drag it, the same as a category.
config.helpWidgetCustomBody:
Every widget above reads something nextDash already knows. The Custom widget reads a figure out of any service that answers with JSON, so a tile can show what your own machines are doing without waiting for nextDash to grow a widget for them. It is deliberately the only one that talks to anything outside.

An address that answers JSON. Any http or https endpoint. GET, or POST for the services that insist. It is fetched by the server, not by your browser — which is what makes a machine on your own network reachable at all, and what keeps a key out of a page any script could read. The address is stored rather than sent: the request names a widget, and the server visits only what that widget was already configured to visit.

Paths into the answer. Name the value you want and nothing else. A path walks objects and arrays — server.disk[0].used — and either names something or does not; a path that silently matched several things would make a wrong figure look right. Up to eight figures on one tile; more than that is a report rather than a glance.

A shape per figure. The same number reads differently depending on what it is: Count, Size, Percentage, Duration, Time ago, Text. Sizes step through KB and MB, a ratio between 0 and 1 is read as a percentage, and a date arrives as seconds, milliseconds or an ISO string.

Or a list instead of figures. Point at an array and the tile draws its entries as rows, up to twenty — the downloads running now, the last few errors.

A sign-in that stays out of your backups. An API key in a header, or a username and password. Credentials are named and reusable, shared with the health checks, and kept in a separate file that no export or backup ZIP includes; the widget itself stores only a reference to one.

Asked on a schedule you set. Anywhere between 30 seconds and a day, five minutes by default. One answer is shared by everyone looking at the dashboard, so a wall display costs the service nothing extra.

What it will not do is change anything. A tile reads, and the two methods it offers are the two that ask a question. An answer has eight seconds to arrive and is read up to a megabyte. There is no expression language and no arithmetic — the moment a config can compute, the config is a second product with its own bugs and no debugger.
config.helpWidgetServicesBody:
Twenty-eight services come filled in: pick one and the address, the figures worth reading and the header its API wants are already there. Everything stays editable afterwards, so a preset is a starting point rather than a lock.

Media & downloads. Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, Readarr, Prowlarr, Bazarr, Overseerr / Jellyseerr, Tautulli, Jellyfin / Emby, Plex, Immich, qBittorrent, SABnzbd, NZBGet.

Network. Pi-hole (v6 and v5 separately, because v6 rewrote its API), AdGuard Home, Traefik, Speedtest Tracker.

System. Proxmox VE, TrueNAS, Glances, Syncthing.

Apps. Nextcloud, Paperless-ngx, Home Assistant, Grafana, ntfy.

What a preset carries. A sample address in the right shape, so you can see what yours should look like; the path on that service that answers with the numbers worth a tile; the figures pulled out of it with their labels and shapes; and how it wants to be signed in to — an X-Api-Key header, a bearer token, a username and password, or nothing at all. Each names where to find its key: Sonarr's is under Settings → General, and the panel tells you so at the moment you need it.

A service that is not on this list needs no code — that is the whole point of the Custom widget. The presets exist because filling in an address, four paths and a header name from another program's documentation is the tedious half, not the hard half.
config.helpArtWidgetTrend: Or the direction it is going
config.helpArtWidgetFetched: Fetched here, never by your browser
config.overviewNewFeatureWidgetFoldTitle: A widget folds away like the categories beside it
config.overviewNewFeatureWidgetFoldWhat: A widget is a summary, and a page carrying several of them has the problem a page of long categories has: the block you want is below the fold because the ones above it are open. Categories have folded since long before widgets existed; a widget could only be dragged, hidden or removed.
config.overviewNewFeatureWidgetFoldHow: Click a widget's title to fold it shut, or press Enter or Space with the header focused — the same gesture on the same header, rather than a second one to learn. Fold all, the . key and the fold-all button take widgets with them, and each block stays folded or open as you left it, per page.
config.overviewNewFeatureStatsReadingTitle: Statistics reports what the app already knows
config.overviewNewFeatureStatsReadingWhat: The section counted bookmarks, tags and categories and stopped there. It said how many services you monitor but never how well they did, nothing about certificates running out, and nothing about how much of the collection has a saved copy — all of which nextDash had already worked out. Some of what it did report was wrong: the healthy share could read 100% directly above a row saying two monitors were down.
config.overviewNewFeatureStatsReadingHow: Health gains uptime over the last day, week and month with the average response and the outages on record; certificates near expiry, counted per site on your own warning window; and how much of the collection has a copy kept here. Content gains a panel for everything that is not a bookmark — widgets, feeds, import sources, the trash and the automatic backups. The healthy share counts every state now, the cleanup score names the threshold you actually set, category panels show names rather than the ids underneath them, and the timestamp follows your 12- or 24-hour setting.
config.overviewNewFeatureStatsReadingEnable: Nothing to switch on. The uptime and certificate panels appear once there is something to report.
config.overviewNewFeatureWidgetCatalogueTitle: Adding a widget no longer loses the widget
config.overviewNewFeatureWidgetCatalogueWhat: The kinds you can add filled a whole screen at the top of the Widgets tab, which pushed the widgets you already have below the fold. Choosing a kind added something you could not see, and the only sign of it was a message in the opposite corner.
config.overviewNewFeatureWidgetCatalogueHow: Widgets opens on your own widgets with one button above them. The catalogue opens over the page, the way the theme browser does, and closes onto the new widget with its name ready to type. The Types tab lists every kind with what it does and adds from there too, and the Custom widget comes with twenty-eight services already filled in.
config.tipTuneThemeBrowser: Config → Appearance → Browse opens the theme browser: 107 families as cards you can search and star, each previewing on the real dashboard while you look at it. Nothing is saved until you pick one.
config.tipMaintStatsUptime: Config → Statistics → Health pools uptime across every monitor over the last day, week and month, and lists certificates close to expiry per site — the readings the health view takes one bookmark at a time.
config.tipDataBeyondBookmarks: Config → Statistics → Content counts what is not a bookmark: how many widgets are on your pages and of what kind, your feeds and import sources, what is waiting in the trash, and how many automatic backups are kept.
config.themeDepthNote: How much of the theme is drawn behind the content: the tint in its greys, the raised surfaces, the wash behind the page. Flat is the dashboard as it was before any of it.
config.backgroundPatternNote: The texture behind the dashboard. Left to the theme, most ask for dots and a few ask for something that suits them. Lines and hatch cover more of the page than dots do, so they read heavier on a light theme.
config.sourceTokenRequired: Paste a token first — this source cannot read anything without one.
config.widgetsDiscardDraftsBody: Your unsaved widget changes on this page will be lost.
config.overviewNewFeatureBrowserHistoryTitle: The browser's Back button moves through nextDash
config.overviewNewFeatureBrowserHistoryWhat: Opening the inbox, health or config, or switching bookmark page, left no trace in the browser's history. Back stripped the address bar and left the view standing, so the URL said one thing and the screen another — and from a view, Back to a bookmarks page did nothing at all.
config.overviewNewFeatureBrowserHistoryHow: Each of those is a history entry now, so Back returns you where you were and Forward brings you back. What counts as a step is deliberately narrow: a filter is not one, so Back leaves the inbox rather than walking through the filters you tried in it, and a config section is not one either, so Back leaves config the way Escape does.
config.overviewNewFeatureBrowserHistoryEnable: Nothing to switch on — it is how the buttons behave now.
config.overviewNewFeatureTriageFinishTitle: A triage run can be finished
config.overviewNewFeatureTriageFinishWhat: The queue held every link the filter showed, including the ones already read, so an inbox of 5 unread and 35 read handed back all forty and asked you to decide again on work already done. The last card looped back to the first rather than ending, and promoting a link closed triage — clearing a backlog of forty meant pressing t forty times.
config.overviewNewFeatureTriageFinishHow: A run now walks the unread only, with the active filter still applying. The last card ends it and says how many you went through. And promoting a link puts you back in the run where you left it, so one t clears the whole backlog.
config.overviewNewFeatureTriageFinishEnable: Press t in the inbox, or use the Triage button above the list.
config.overviewNewFeatureListHeadersTitle: The inbox and health lists start where the rows do
config.overviewNewFeatureListHeadersWhat: Both views put a wall of controls between their heading and their first row: ten bordered summary tiles, a filter strip that scrolled sideways with four filters past its right edge, and eight action buttons across two lines. On a laptop the first bookmark sat below the fold.
config.overviewNewFeatureListHeadersHow: The tiles read as one compact line, the filters wrap so every one of them is on screen, and the actions you rarely use moved behind a ⋯ — Work through and Triage stay where they are. The two views were changed to match each other, so switching between them no longer means learning a second layout.
config.overviewNewFeatureWidgetTourTitle: A tour of what a custom widget can reach
config.overviewNewFeatureWidgetTourWhat: The Custom widget can read any address that answers with JSON, which is the most capable thing in the Widgets section and the hardest to discover: nothing on the page said what it could do or where to start.
config.overviewNewFeatureWidgetTourHow: Seven steps, opening the first time you visit Config → Widgets. It walks the catalogue of ready-made services, the fields a custom widget maps, and how a figure gets from an endpoint onto your page. Ask for it again from Behavior → General → Onboarding.
config.overviewNewFeatureWidgetTourEnable: Opens by itself on a first visit to Widgets.
config.overviewNewFeatureWidgetFigureSizeTitle: Every figure on a custom widget can have its own size
config.overviewNewFeatureWidgetFigureSizeWhat: A tile whose numbers were all drawn the same size left you to work out which one mattered. The custom widget drew flat rows where every other tile gave its main figure room, so the number you built the tile for looked exactly like the ones giving it context.
config.overviewNewFeatureWidgetFigureSizeHow: Each figure is now Normal, Large, Small or a Bar, set per figure when you add or edit it. The bar is offered on a percentage, where a share of a whole is something it can draw, and it takes its colour from the theme you are using.
config.overviewNewFeatureWidgetFigureSizeEnable: Nothing to switch on — open a custom widget and edit one of its figures.
config.overviewNewFeatureShortcutDisplayTitle: The shortcut letters are on, and have a third setting
config.overviewNewFeatureShortcutDisplayWhat: The shortcut letters were on or off. On, they sat in a column of their own down the right of every category — as loud as the bookmark names beside them, and holding the width that made those names truncate. Off, you lost the reminder of what your own shortcuts are, and some dashboards had lost them years ago without meaning to.
config.overviewNewFeatureShortcutDisplayHow: There is a third answer now: the letter floats in over the end of the name while your pointer or keyboard selection is on that row. Nothing moves when it appears, and the names get about five characters of width back.
config.overviewNewFeatureShortcutDisplayEnable: Config → Appearance → Shortcut letters on rows.
config.overviewNewFeatureSearchNameHintTitle: A search that finds nothing says where to look
config.overviewNewFeatureSearchNameHintWhat: Typing a bookmark's name into the search overlay reported nothing found while the bookmark sat on the page behind it. A plain query looks for a shortcut, not a name, and the overlay never said so.
config.overviewNewFeatureSearchNameHintHow: When there is nothing by that shortcut but something by that name, the overlay adds one line saying how many bookmarks carry it, and Enter runs the search the other way. When nothing matches either, “nothing found” stays the answer.
config.overviewNewFeatureSearchNameHintEnable: Nothing to switch on — it is how search answers now.
config.overviewNewFeatureSearchModeKeyTitle: The search mode has a key of its own
config.overviewNewFeatureSearchModeKeyWhat: Whether typing letters finds a bookmark's name or its shortcut was a tickbox under Appearance → Layout labelled “Interleave categories across columns” — which is not what it does. Nothing about the layout has ever read it, so ticking it to rearrange your columns changed how typing was read and moved nothing on screen.
config.overviewNewFeatureSearchModeKeyHow: It sits under Behavior → Search now, called Switch Search Mode, and Shift + Q flips it from the dashboard itself with a message saying which way it landed — for the times you want the other mode for a single search.
config.overviewNewFeatureSearchModeKeyEnable: Nothing to switch on — Shift + Q works from any bookmark page.
config.overviewNewFeatureChineseWhat: 简体中文 joins English, Dutch, German and French as a fifth full language — and it is the whole of it, not a partial pass. The dashboard and its cheat sheet, the command palette, the setup wizards, every config tab, the statistics, the health view and its reasons, and all 209 headings of the Help tab.
config.overviewNewFeatureChineseHow: Pick it under Appearance → Language. Nothing falls back to English on the way through, and the theme browser — a screen that had stayed English in every language — was translated with it.
config.overviewNewFeatureChineseEnable: Nothing to switch on — choose the language and the whole interface follows.
config.overviewNewFeatureSearchGroupsTitle: Search groups its results, and learns which one you meant
config.overviewNewFeatureSearchGroupsWhat: One letter used to fill the screen. Typing g put Gmail and widGetonderzoek in the same column, in the same style, in an order nothing on screen explained — and the ranking looked the same on your thousandth search as on your first.
config.overviewNewFeatureSearchGroupsHow: Results now group by why they matched: the strong ones stay open, the rest fold behind a heading and a count, and nothing is thrown away. The ranking reads how often you open a bookmark and remembers which result you picked for the keystrokes you picked it with, so mail can become your own alias for Gmail without a shortcut for it.
config.overviewNewFeatureSearchGroupsEnable: Nothing to switch on — open the search and type.

colors.title: theme customization
colors.saveColorsInfoMessage:
Two separate save actions:

• Save colors (this tab) — writes palette edits from the Theme tab to the server. Use this after changing hex values or adding/removing custom themes.

• Save (config header) — stores General settings: which theme is active, layout, bookmarks, language, etc. It does not save color hex values from this tab.

Typical flow: edit colors → Save colors → pick the theme under General → Appearance → Save in the header.

featureTour.step7Body: Use arrow keys to navigate, Enter to open and ; to edit inline. Drag via the narrow handle strip on the left to reorder. In Config → Bookmarks you manage everything in bulk, import and export.
featureTour.step8Body: The tour is complete. All features are fully configurable via Config: themes, layout version (Classic or Modern), layout presets, finders, smart collections and bookmark management.
